LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.

1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

A A PPENDIX

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset

given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.
excerpts.heading: 2 M ETHODS & R ESULTS

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

1

over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat

on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

We build upon the approach presented in SSD (Foster et al., 2023). Given the parameter importance
over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

meaning this is only calculated once, and then the train-set may be discarded after. We replace
the Fisher information with the sensitivity estimation from Aljundi et al. (2018), which we now

of the gradient. For multi-dimensional outputs, this gradient must be calculated over every dimen-

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

A A PPENDIX

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

expectations: identify the paper's method before applying method-specific criteria

synthesis.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Label-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD), an extension of the authors' Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) method for retraining-free machine unlearning. LFSSD replaces SSD's Fisher-information-diagonal parameter importance with the output-sensitivity estimate from Aljundi et al. (2018), the gradient of the squared l2 norm of the model output. Because this estimate needs no labels or loss, only unlabelled forget samples are needed at forgetting time, given importance over the full training data computed once beforehand. The method is evaluated against SSD and a retrain reference on class, subclass, and random-sample unlearning with ResNet and ViT models on CIFAR benchmarks.
synthesis.originality: The contribution is incremental and the paper positions it honestly. It is a component substitution that brings a continual-learning importance estimator (Aljundi et al., 2018) into the SSD framework (Foster et al.), and both components are attributed to prior work. The originality lies in this combination and in the label-free property at forgetting time, not in a new importance measure. Two originality claims are not established by the paper itself. First, the statement that output-sensitivity importance 'has not been applied in unlearning' is an absence claim with no supporting survey, and we could not assess it. Second, the claim that LFSSD is the 'first retraining-free unlearning method to require only the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time' is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. It rests on a brief related-work discussion confined to the introduction, and it does not engage label- or data-light alternatives such as zero-shot unlearning, which is cited only in passing. The scope of 'first' should be stated precisely: the label-free property holds at forgetting time, while computing importance over D still requires the full training data, as SSD also does. If prior unlearning work has already used MAS-style importance, the novelty of the substitution would shrink further.
synthesis.likely_impact: Practitioners who must honour forget requests without ground-truth labels could benefit from a simple, retraining-free option. The paper's motivating examples are unlabelled catalogues and models trained with semi-supervised learning, where pseudo labels may be unreliable. Its simplicity suits the tiny-paper format and makes it easy to adopt within SSD-style pipelines. Several factors may limit its influence. The motivating label-free scenarios are not evaluated, and all experiments use labelled datasets. Selecting the dampening hyperparameter α appears to require measuring retain and forget accuracy, which needs labels, and this partly undercuts the label-free motivation in deployment. Finally, effectiveness relative to the retrain reference is uneven on subclass forgetting.
synthesis.decision_synthesis: On the positive side, the method is a clearly scoped, cleanly motivated modification. The label-free property holds by construction, since the importance estimate uses no labels and the training set can be discarded after a one-time importance computation. The comparison with SSD broadly supports comparable behaviour on class unlearning. On the negative side, the evidence that matters most concerns the central claim that the new importance estimate is 'equally effective as Fisher information'. In subclass unlearning, LFSSD's forget-set accuracy departs substantially from the retrain reference in several cases. For ViT 'sea', retrain keeps about 95% forget accuracy while LFSSD drops it to about 21%. For ResNet 'sea', the figures are about 91% for retrain versus about 18% for LFSSD. This is the over-forgetting the paper itself warns about. For ViT 'mushroom', LFSSD and SSD deviate from retrain in opposite directions. No aggregate distance-to-retrain metric is reported. SSD and LFSSD were also tuned with different procedures and different per-setting α values (for example α = 10, 5, and 3.5 for LFSSD across settings). The sensitivity analysis covers only CIFAR100 rocket-class unlearning, so differences may mix the effect of the importance measure with the effect of tuning. Score-changing questions for the authors: (1) How were α values chosen for each setting, and would a single α (e.g., 10) work across all benchmarks? (2) Can the comparison be repeated under matched hyperparameter tuning, with a summary metric of distance to retrain? (3) How should α be chosen in a genuinely label-free deployment? (4) Can the 'first' and 'not applied in unlearning' claims be scoped precisely and supported with broader related work, including zero-shot and data-free unlearning? Non-blocking improvements: evaluate a scenario with noisy or pseudo labels to support the practical motivation, and restate the effectiveness claim to distinguish class from subclass results.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In the second quoted row (Cifar100 lamp, ViT), LFSSD reaches 0.00 Df while SSD retains 36.89, which favours LFSSD. In the first row (ViT mushroom subclass), LFSSD's Df of 31.42 is above SSD's 6.68 and close to retrain's 26.57, so it is retrain-like there. Results vary by class. The supporting claims also include a primacy claim and practicality claims that rest on argument rather than measurement.
points: The results broadly support competitiveness with SSD, but the claim of being 'similar to retrain' is uneven, notably on ViT subclass unlearning.

significance.reasoning: The authors name concrete deployment scenarios in which labels are unavailable.
points: The paper targets a practically relevant setting: unlearning without stored retain data or labels, such as copyright catalogues or semi-supervised models.

originality.reasoning: The authors attribute both building blocks to prior work: the dampening rule comes from SSD and the importance estimator from Aljundi et al. The original element is therefore the combination and its application to unlearning. That combination removes the label requirement, which is a useful and clearly stated difference. Whether the estimator has truly never been used in unlearning is author-reported and was not verified here. The primacy claim is hedged in the introduction but stated unhedged in the conclusion. The related-work discussion covers only a few retraining-free methods.
points: LFSSD's novelty is a targeted transfer: it swaps SSD's Fisher-based importance for the MAS output-sensitivity estimate (Aljundi et al., 2018). The authors frame it as an extension, not a new paradigm.
The paper claims to be the 'first' method with no labels and no retraining, but positions itself only against FisherForgetting, SSD and retraining-based methods.

claim_support.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The authors say the estimator comes from prior work (author-reported) and claim novelty only for its application to SSD-style unlearning. Whether it was truly unapplied in unlearning was not independently verified. The estimator itself is attributed to prior work. What is new is using it inside SSD's selection and dampening rule.
points: The authors present the novelty as transferring an existing continual-learning importance estimator into unlearning, not as a new estimator. This candid positioning makes the claimed advance narrow but clearly bounded.

The swap of Fisher information for the gradient of the l2 output norm is the core technical change. The paper credits Aljundi et al. (2018) for this estimator, so the novelty lies only in applying it to SSD.

claim_support.reasoning: On ViT lamp, SSD leaves 36.89% Df accuracy while LFSSD reaches 0. In face unlearning, LFSSD's MIA (0.38) is lower than SSD's (1.11). The evaluation includes the retrain gold standard and the closest prior method (SSD), which are the comparisons a reader most needs to judge the contribution.
points: Class and face unlearning results support competitiveness with SSD. LFSSD reaches 0% Df accuracy with Dr close to SSD, and sometimes beats SSD, e.g. on ViT lamp.
The tables support the empirical-evaluation contribution across class, subclass, random and face unlearning with multiple baselines.

display.title: Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD) unlearning method
display.summary: An extension of Selective Synaptic Dampening that replaces Fisher-information-based parameter importance with the gradient of the squared l2 norm of the model output. This removes the need for the loss or ground-truth labels while keeping unlearning retraining-free.

claim_support.reasoning: No claims are linked to this contribution, so its claim support cannot be traced. The two rows show forget-set accuracy. On ViT lamp (Cifar100) and ViT ED (Cifar20), SSD leaves residual Df accuracy (36.89 and 53.53), while LFSSD reaches 0.00 and 0.68. The tables also cover full-class, subclass and random forgetting with retrain and finetune baselines. On ViT lamp unlearning, LFSSD reaches Df 0.00 versus 36.89 for SSD, while Dr accuracy is retained. This supports competitiveness. In the ViT lamp class experiment, Df accuracy is 0.00 for LFSSD versus 36.89 for SSD. Retain accuracy (Dr) is comparable across the two methods. In the ViT subclass 'sea' row, retrain gives Df 95.12 but LFSSD gives 20.83. Since the paper itself treats closeness to retrain as the target, this indicates over-forgetting relative to SSD (97.05). The benchmark is broad for a tiny paper, covering two architectures and three task types.
points: Across the reported benchmarks, LFSSD is broadly competitive with SSD. It sometimes improves on SSD's ViT failure cases, which supports the competitiveness claim.
The empirical results across ResNet18 and ViT, multiple tasks, and multiple baselines broadly support the claim that LFSSD is competitive with SSD.
The results tables support the claim that LFSSD is competitive with SSD. In some ViT settings LFSSD forgets more completely than SSD, but subclass forget accuracy varies from SSD and from retraining.
The claim of being 'equally effective as Fisher information' is not uniform: ViT subclass results show sizable deviations from retrain on Df.
None of the candidate contributions has linked supporting claims. The empirical support comes from Tables 1 and 3–7, which compare LFSSD with SSD and baselines across 10 runs.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: Both components are attributed to prior work: SSD to Foster et al. and the sensitivity estimator to Aljundi et al. The contribution is their combination and the label-free property it yields. The paper frames this honestly as an extension. The cited works' content is author-reported here and was not independently verified. The claim is scoped as an extension of SSD, so it does not overclaim. Both components are attributed to prior work. The claimed difference is transferring the estimator to unlearning. That this has not been done before is author-reported and not verified here.
points: The authors present LFSSD as an extension of their prior SSD method. The only change is that the Fisher-diagonal importance term is replaced with the Memory Aware Synapses output-sensitivity estimate from Aljundi et al. (2018). The novelty is therefore a component substitution, and the authors describe it as such.
The paper calls LFSSD 'a novel extension of SSD', which matches its stated positioning as a modification of SSD.

The authors frame LFSSD as an extension that combines their prior SSD with an importance estimator they attribute to Aljundi et al. (2018). The novelty lies in this combination and its application to unlearning, not in a new estimator.

claim_support.reasoning: No claims are linked to this contribution, so its claim support cannot be traced. Because importance over D is computed once and the train set can then be discarded, only unlabelled Df inputs are needed at forgetting time. This supports the mechanism part of the claim, but not the primacy part. The motivating scenario is described but not tested. The claim is valid at forgetting time only. Precomputation over D is still required.
points: The 'first label-free' contribution has no linked supporting claims. The paper does substantiate that the method needs only unlabelled forget inputs at forgetting time, by noting that importance over D is computed once beforehand.

The label-free claim is substantiated by construction, since Eq. 3 uses no labels. However, all experiments use labelled datasets, and the motivating label-free scenarios (catalogues, semi-supervised models) are not evaluated.
Computing importance over D still requires the training inputs once, which tempers the 'only unlabelled forget samples' framing.

significance.reasoning: The authors provide plausible use cases for label-free unlearning.
points: Removing label and retain-set dependence is practically useful, and the authors motivate concrete label-free scenarios.

originality.reasoning: The paper cites Chundawat 2023b (zero-shot unlearning) only in a list of retraining-based methods. It does not explain why that method or similar ones fall outside the 'first' claim. The related-work discussion is confined to a single combined introduction section. Without a broader survey of label-free or source-free unlearning, the 'first' claim cannot be checked from the paper alone. SSD also precomputes over D, so storage of D is not the difference. The difference is the label requirement. The paper does not discuss zero-shot unlearning (Chundawat 2023b, cited only in passing) as a label- or data-light alternative. The priority claim rests only on the authors' own survey, which cites a small set of prior methods.
points: The 'first' claim for retraining-free unlearning with unlabelled forget samples is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. The paper does not discuss zero-shot or other data-light unlearning methods to show they need labels.

The primacy claim ('first retraining-free method requiring only unlabelled forget samples') is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. However, the related-work coverage behind it is very brief and does not address label-free or zero-shot unlearning work beyond what is cited.
The 'first' claim depends on storing a precomputed importance over D. The label-free requirement applies only at forgetting time, since computing the D importance needs access to the full data.

The claim that LFSSD is 'the first' retraining-free method needing only unlabelled forget samples is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. The paper's related-work coverage is brief, so this priority claim is unverified.

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.

author_originality_statements.statement: Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm, substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity.
